title: Nutritional prehabilitation in head and neck cancer
official: To investigate the feasibility of a co-produced nutritional prehabilitation intervention for head and neck cancer (HNC) patients treated with radical radiotherapy (+/- chemotherapy)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Each year, more than 12,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with head and neck cancer. Many people are diagnosed when their cancer is already advanced. Some have already lost more than 10% of their body weight and may be malnourished. People with head and neck cancer may also have other health conditions or find it harder to stay healthy because of lifestyle or financial pressures. Treatment often involves daily radiotherapy for 6 to 7 weeks. Radiotherapy to the mouth and throat can cause strong side effects, such as severe pain and problems swallowing. Some people need a feeding tube so they can get enough food and fluids during treatment and recovery. People may continue to lose weight during and after treatment. This weight loss can make people weaker and may stop them doing everyday activities they want or need to do. Earlier support before treatment may help people manage eating and drinking problems and reduce weight loss. This support can include advice about nutrition, physical health and emotional wellbeing. This is often called prehabilitation. This research will bring together people who have had head and neck cancer, their partners or carers, and health professionals. They will discuss their experiences of nutrition and preparing for cancer treatment. The group will look at ways to improve nutrition care before patients start radiotherapy treatment. Together, they will agree on a possible solution(s) and help create it. The solution(s) will then be tested with new patients having radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, for head and neck cancer. Patients will be asked what they think about it. 

Who can participate? 
Work package 1: co-production 
People who have completed treatment for head and neck cancer may take part. Partners and carers of people with head and neck cancer may also take part. Health professionals who work with people with head and neck cancer may take part. This includes dietitians, speech and language therapists, radiographers, and physiotherapists. Head and neck clinical nurse specialists may take part. Head and neck doctors may take part. This includes oncologists, surgeons, and anesthetists. Members of head and neck clinical quality groups, cancer alliances or other relevant groups may also take part. 
  
Work package 2: feasibility study 
Adults aged 18 years or over may take part. They must have head and neck cancer and be due to have radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, to try to cure the cancer.They must be able to understand the study and give consent. 

What does the study involve?
The project has two parts and will run over 3 years. 
1. Co-production and co-creation:
This part will involve workshops with people who have had head and neck cancer, their partners or carers, and health professionals who support people with head and neck cancer. These people will be invited from across the UK and will be called co-creation participants. In the workshops, participants will talk about the challenges of eating, drinking and preparing for treatment. They will agree on a solution, and work together with the the research team to create it. The solution will be called Co-ENHANCE. 
2. Feasibility study:
This part will test whether Co-ENHANCE is practical and helpful for newly diagnosed patients receiving radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy. Co-ENHANCE will be offered during a dietitian appointment, in the way agreed by the co-creation group. People who receive Co-ENHANCE, and people who choose not to receive it, may be invited to a short interview to share their views. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of taking part? 
Possible benefits:
1. Patients and carers can share their experiences of head and neck cancer and nutrition
2. People may feel more involved because they are helping to design the support
3. Patients in the feasibility study may get earlier and more detailed nutrition support
4. Patients may feel better prepared and learn how to improve their nutrition before radiotherapy
Possible risks:
1. Some people may feel upset during workshops when talking about personal experiences
2. Some people may feel less confident speaking openly when patients and health professionals are in the same group
3. Taking part may add extra time or effort for patients
4. Body composition tests are not recommended for people who are pregnant or who have an implanted electronic device, such as a pacemaker. These people will not have bioelectrical impedance analysis

Where is the study run from? 
University of Liverpool (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2025 to August 2027

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Linda Cantwell, linda.cantwell@liverpool.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Work package 1:
1.  HNC patients who have completed curative treatment for HNC 
2. Caregivers of HNC patients
3. HNC or oncology prehabilitation AHPs (i.e. dietitians,speech and language therapist,radiographers,physiotherapist)
4. HNC or oncology prehabilitation clinical nurse specialists
5. Head and neck consultants or trainees–oncologist,surgeons,anaesthetists
6. Members of HNC Clinical Quality Groups (CQG) including cancer alliance or other stakeholders/decision makers involved with HNC or oncology prehabilitation services
7. Persons living/working within the UK

Work package 2: 
1. ≥18 years
2. Able to provide informed consent
3. Diagnosed with HNC for treatment with curative intent
4. Referred for adjunctive or primary CRT
Exclusion criteria:
Work package 1:
1. Persons who lack capacity to provide informed consent 
2. Persons who would require an English language interpreter 

Work package 2: 
1. Refeeding syndrome
2. Hospital admittance required for intense nutrition support or other clinical reason i.e. alcohol detox
3. Palliative treatment
